text: A constant-product AMM isn't just a formula — it's actual code. This lesson puts Lesson 5's x times y equals k, and Lesson 6's LP-token math, into a real, minimal Solidity contract, line by line.

The addLiquidity function mints LP tokens proportional to what you deposit. The very first deposit into an empty pool is special — it bootstraps the price ratio, since there's nothing yet to be proportional to. Every deposit after that mints the smaller of the two ratios, so one side can't unfairly dilute the other.

swapAForB is where the math becomes code. The 0.3% fee comes off the input amount first, in amountAfterFee, before the constant-product formula ever runs — k equals reserveA times reserveB. That ordering is deliberate: it's exactly how the fee ends up staying in the pool's reserves instead of being skimmed off separately.

Three lines carry the whole lesson. k equals reserveA times reserveB is Lesson 5's invariant, word for word. The fee comes off before the formula runs, which is how it stays in the reserves. And the proportional LP minting in addLiquidity is Lesson 6's token math, just written in Solidity instead of worked by hand.

This contract is deliberately incomplete. It has no reentrancy guard, no slippage protection, never moves real ERC-20 tokens, and its LP balance isn't a tradeable token. Every one of those gaps is load-bearing in a real deployment — this version exists to make the formulas concrete, not to be deployed.
Next: concentrated liquidity, and why spreading capital evenly across every possible price, the way this contract does, usually isn't the most efficient use of it.
